plain_text:
To celebrate the launch of Getty's Digital Florentine Codex—
an enhanced online edition of the encyclopedic 16th-century
manuscript of early colonial Mexican and Nahua knowledge—
Getty and LAist co-hosted a night of musical performances.
The Getty Research Institute's Kim Richter and LAist reporter
Adolfo Guzman-Lopez introduced the event, highlighting the
codex's significance to the local region and to humanity itself.

The Getty Research Institute's Kim Richter and LAist reporter Adolfo Guzman-Lopez introduced the event, highlighting the codex's significance to the local region and to humanity itself.

plain_text:
Musical group Xochi Cuicat opened the performance with
original compositions using string and percussion instruments
of Mesoamerica and Mexico.

plain_text:
Musician Lu Coy, along with guitarist Jonathan Alma-
raz, debuted an original score directly inspired by the ancient
knowledge within the recently digitized manuscript. Audience
members were treated to an immersive, sensory experience
inspired by the sights and sounds of early colonial Indigenous
Mexico.

plain_text:
The evening concluded with Coy in the fountain, which
symbolized Aztec moon goddess Coyoizauhqui's domain above
the aquatic underworld. When asked what the audience might
take away from the performance, Coy answered, “the experi-
ence of being with our ancestors—who are lonely and longing
to have time spent with them.” As Richter said, “This is not a
dead history. The descendants of the Nahua and Mexica are
among us.”

plain_text:
On October 7The Getty Research Institute welcomed
more than 600 visitors to a celebration of South-
ern California's Indigenous cultural heritage. The
day's sevents, led by Getty and local partners, included
live performances, workshops, and a custom tasting
menu. Meztl Projects organized a linocut-stamp
workshop inspired by motifs in the Florentine
Codex. Posters with illustrations by Westhyot
Alvibre encouraged visitors to find the endangered
white sage plant and other California natives at the
Getty Center, which is sited on the tribal land of the
Tonga/Gabriliano people.

Meztl Projects organized a linocut-stamp workshop inspired by motifs in the Florentine Codex. Posters with illustrations by Westhyot Alvibre encouraged visitors to find the endangered white sage plant and other California natives at the Getty Center, which is sited on the tribal land of the Tonga/Gabriliano people.

plain_text:
In the garden, musicians Carmina Escobar,
Micaela Tobin, and Jacqueline Wilson performed
scores written by Pulitzer Prize-winning artist and
composer Raven Chacon, who originally dedicated
them to Indigenous female composers and musi-
cians. Back on the plaza, guests sampled traditional
Mesoamerican cuisine selected by culinary anthro-
pologist Claudia Serrato. Ingredients included cacao,
amaranth, and native bay leaves. "This is so cool—it's
the food our ancestors ate!" said one teenager, testi-
fying to food's unique power across generations and
cultures.
